verification.reasoning: Six months at $3,240 — the target as it stands today.
Five years of compounding at 3.2% on $3,240. The reserve target is defined by spending, so it moves when spending does.
Six months at the year-5 spending level of $3,792.66 — the target the reserve has to reach, not the one it was set against.
Five years at 0.8% — the reserve grows, just far more slowly than the spending it exists to cover.
$22,755.96 needed against $20,230.14 held — a reserve that was fully funded is now short without a dollar ever leaving it.
$2,525.82 against the $22,755.96 target — the reserve has lost about a ninth of its coverage in five years.
$20,230.14 against $3,792.66 of monthly spending — the six-month reserve has quietly become a 5.3-month one.
$2,525.82 spread across 5 years — the maintenance cost of keeping a reserve at its stated coverage.

levels.label: Not yet

levels.descriptor: Uncertainty is mentioned in general terms only.

levels.label: Approaching

levels.label: Meets
levels.descriptor: Every stated criterion is applied and the result of each is reported.

levels.label: Exceeds
levels.descriptor: Every criterion is applied and the response says which one decided the outcome.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.descriptor: The parts of the plan contradict each other or do not add up.

levels.label: Approaching
levels.descriptor: The plan adds up but one part is not connected to the rest.

levels.label: Meets
levels.descriptor: The plan adds up and each part is consistent with the others and with the constraint.

levels.label: Exceeds
levels.descriptor: The plan adds up, is internally consistent, and states what would break it first.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.descriptor: A conclusion is stated with no figures behind it.

levels.descriptor: Figures are quoted but the step from figure to conclusion is missing.

levels.label: Meets
levels.descriptor: The response shows which figures drive the conclusion and how.

levels.label: Exceeds
levels.descriptor: The response also says how large a change in a figure would flip the conclusion.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.descriptor: A choice is asserted with no cost acknowledged.

levels.label: Approaching
levels.descriptor: A choice is defended but what it gives up is not named.

levels.label: Meets
levels.descriptor: The choice is defended and what it costs or forecloses is named specifically.

levels.label: Exceeds
levels.descriptor: The choice is defended, its cost is named, and the strongest case against it is answered.

judgment.prompt: Aisha’s reserve was fully funded, nothing was withdrawn, and it is short. Explain the mechanism, and say what it means to describe a reserve as "six months" rather than as a dollar amount.
acceptableAnswerCriteria: Explains that the target is defined by spending, which rises at 3.2%, while the reserve grows at only 0.8%, so the two drift apart with no withdrawal required.
Argues that stating a reserve in months of coverage keeps the target attached to what it protects, whereas a dollar amount silently shrinks in coverage as prices rise.
Uses the 5.3-month figure to show what the drift amounts to in the terms the household actually cares about.
evidenceRequirements: Cites the 3.2% and 0.8% rates as the two figures that pull the target and the reserve apart.
lookFors: The response identifies the drift as arising from two different rates, not from spending the reserve.
The response prefers coverage to a dollar figure and says why.
A response noting the reserve did grow, just too slowly, is reading the figures accurately.
judgment.commonMisconception: Treating a savings target set once as a target that stays correct.

judgment.prompt: A reserve has to be available at short notice, which is why it earns only 0.8%. Say what that constraint costs Aisha over the five years, and whether a higher-earning account would be a good place for this money.
acceptableAnswerCriteria: Prices the constraint using the figures: the $2,525.82 shortfall, or the $505.16 a year needed to maintain coverage, is what the liquidity requirement costs.
Argues that a reserve should stay accessible even at a lower return, because a reserve that cannot be reached on the day it is needed has failed at its only job.
evidenceRequirements: Refers to the $2,525.82 shortfall or the $505.16 annual top-up when pricing the constraint.
lookFors: The response prices the tradeoff rather than treating the low return as simply bad.
The response ties accessibility to the purpose of the reserve, not to a general rule.
judgment.commonMisconception: Judging where to hold a reserve on its return alone.
